content: Condoms can be made from various materials, including latex, polyurethane, polyisoprene, lambskin, and nitrile. They function by creating a barrier that prevents sperm from entering the vagina, thereby avoiding pregnancy. Additionally, they help prevent the transmission of infections present in semen, on the penis, or in the vagina from one partner to the other. Effectiveness of Condoms: The effectiveness of condoms depends on consistent and correct use. The risk of pregnancy or sexually transmitted infections (STIs) is highest when condoms are not used during every sexual act. Incorrect use, slippage, or breakage rarely leads to pregnancy or infection. Pregnancy Prevention: With typical use, about 13 pregnancies occur per 100 women whose partners use male condoms in the first year. This means 87 out of 100 women will not become pregnant. With perfect use (correct use during every sexual act), about 2 pregnancies occur per 100 women in the first year. Protection Against STIs and HIV: Male condoms significantly reduce the risk of HIV transmission when used correctly and consistently during vaginal or anal sex. They prevent 80–95% of HIV transmissions that would have occurred without condom use. Condoms also reduce the risk of many other STIs, including those spread by discharge (e.g., gonorrhea, chlamydia) and skin-to-skin contact (e.g., herpes, HPV). Usage Guidelines: 1. Use a new condom for each sexual act. Check the package for damage and expiration date. Open the package carefully to avoid tearing the condom. 2. Place the condom on the tip of the erect penis before any genital, oral, or anal contact. 3. Unroll the condom to the base of the penis. If it does not unroll easily, it may be backward, damaged, or too old. Discard and use a new one. 4. After ejaculation, hold the condom's rim in place and withdraw the penis while still erect. Avoid spilling semen. 5. Dispose of the used condom safely by wrapping it and placing it in the trash. Do not flush it down the toilet. Important Considerations: Do not use oil-based lubricants with latex condoms, as they can cause damage. Avoid reusing condoms or using multiple condoms simultaneously. Use a new condom when switching between different sexual acts (e.g., anal to vaginal sex) to prevent bacterial transfer. Female Condoms: Female condoms are thin, soft sheaths with flexible rings at both ends. They are inserted into the vagina and work by forming a barrier to prevent sperm from entering. They also reduce the risk of STIs, including HIV, when used correctly and consistently. Pregnancy Prevention: With typical use, about 21 pregnancies occur per 100 women in the first year. This means 79 out of 100 women will not become pregnant. With perfect use, about 5 pregnancies occur per 100 women in the first year. Usage Instructions: 1. Use a new female condom for each sexual act. 2. Insert the condom into the vagina before any genital contact. It can be inserted up to 8 hours before sex. 3. 4. After sex, twist the outer ring to seal fluids and gently remove the condom. 5. Dispose of the condom safely. Male Sterilization (Vasectomy): Vasectomy is a permanent contraceptive method for men who do not want more children. It involves cutting or blocking the vas deferens (the tubes that carry sperm) to prevent sperm from entering the semen. The procedure is highly effective, with less than 1 pregnancy per 100 women in the first year after the procedure. However, it takes about 3 months for the vasectomy to become fully effective, so alternative contraception should be used during this time. Reversibility: Vasectomy is intended to be permanent. Reversal surgery is difficult, expensive, and often unsuccessful. Protection Against STIs: Vasectomy does not protect against STIs. Female Sterilization: Female sterilization, also known as tubal ligation, is a permanent surgical method for women who do not want more children. It involves blocking or cutting the fallopian tubes to prevent eggs from meeting sperm. The procedure is highly effective, with less than 1 pregnancy per 100 women in the first year. Reversibility: Like vasectomy, female sterilization is intended to be permanent. Reversal is difficult and often unsuccessful. Protection Against STIs: Female sterilization does not protect against STIs. Withdrawal Method: The withdrawal method, or pulling out, involves the man withdrawing his penis from the vagina before ejaculation to prevent sperm from entering the woman's body. This method is less effective than other contraceptive methods, with about 20 pregnancies per 100 women in the first year of typical use. With perfect use, about 4 pregnancies occur per 100 women. Protection Against STIs: The withdrawal method does not protect against STIs. Considerations: Men must be able to predict ejaculation accurately for this method to be effective. General Advice: For all contraceptive methods, proper use and consistency are key to maximizing effectiveness. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) can be used if a method fails (e.g., condom breakage or failure to withdraw in time). Individuals should seek medical advice if they experience complications or have concerns about their chosen method.
